headline: Burnham says the UK-EU 'status quo' is not good enough as he sets out agenda for 20 November Brussels summit

terms.meaning: The EU trading area where goods and services move freely between members with common rules.

levels.headline: Burnham says the UK-EU 'status quo' is not good enough as he sets out agenda for 20 November Brussels summit
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham told MPs on 12 October that sticking with the current relationship with the European Union is 'not good enough' and that refusing to explore a closer one would be a 'major dereliction of duty'. He confirmed that a UK-EU summit will be held in Brussels on 20 November.
The agenda includes a trade deal on food and drink products, a deal on emissions trading, the linking of energy systems, a youth experience scheme and deeper cooperation on immigration. Mr Burnham said a successful summit is his first priority, with a longer-term discussion about the wider options to follow.
In a BBC interview he said a referendum would not be right at present but did not rule one out in future. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused him of 'unpicking' the withdrawal agreement, while the MEP Bernd Lange has floated a 'Switzerland plus' arrangement that could be negotiated within months once a decision to deepen ties is made.
The UK left the EU in 2020, and this autumn marks ten years since the 2016 referendum, which keeps the question politically sensitive.
levels.why: The summit will test how far the government can rebuild trade and other ties with the UK's biggest neighbour.

levels.headline: Burnham says current UK-EU relationship 'not good enough' and confirms 20 November summit in Brussels
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the Commons on 12 October that the present relationship with the European Union is 'not good enough'. He said it would be a 'major dereliction of duty' to refuse even to look at closer ties. A UK-EU summit will take place in Brussels on 20 November.
Talks are expected to cover food and drink trade, emissions trading, links between energy systems, a youth experience scheme and closer work on immigration. Mr Burnham said a good result at the summit comes first, and a longer conversation about wider options would follow.
He told the BBC that a referendum is not the right step now, though he did not rule one out later. The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, said he was 'unpicking' the withdrawal agreement. The MEP Bernd Lange has suggested a 'Switzerland plus' deal, which could be agreed within months once both sides decide to go ahead.
The issue is delicate because the UK voted to leave the EU in 2016 and formally left in 2020.
levels.why: It could change how easily British firms and people trade, travel and work with Europe.

levels.headline: Burnham wants closer EU ties and says the 'status quo' is not good enough
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has told MPs that the UK's current relationship with the European Union is not good enough. He said it would be a serious failure of duty not to explore a closer one. A summit between the UK and the EU will be held in Brussels on 20 November.
The agenda includes a deal on food and drink trade, a scheme for carbon pricing known as emissions trading, joining up energy systems, a youth experience scheme and more cooperation on immigration. Mr Burnham says getting a good outcome from the summit is his first aim. A longer talk about wider options will come afterwards.
He has said a new referendum is not right at the moment, but he has not ruled one out for the future. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch says he is 'unpicking' the deal that took the UK out of the EU. A senior European politician, Bernd Lange, has suggested a 'Switzerland plus' deal.
The UK left the EU in 2020, so the topic is still a sensitive one.
levels.why: Closer ties could affect trade, prices and travel for people across the UK.

levels.headline: Burnham says UK's current deal with the EU is not good enough ahead of November summit
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on 12 October that the UK's current relationship with the European Union is not good enough. He told MPs it would be a major failure of duty to refuse to look at a closer one. The two sides will meet at a summit in Brussels on 20 November.
Topics for the summit include a trade deal on food and drink, a system for pricing carbon emissions, linking energy supplies, a youth experience scheme and cooperation on immigration. Mr Burnham says a successful summit comes first, and then there will be a longer discussion about other choices.
He said a new referendum is not the right thing to do now, but he did not rule one out later. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said he was 'unpicking' the agreement that took the UK out of the EU. Bernd Lange, a member of the European Parliament, has suggested a 'Switzerland plus' deal.
Britain voted to leave in 2016 and left in 2020, so any move back towards the EU is politically sensitive.
levels.why: The talks could make trade with Europe easier, which affects prices and jobs.

levels.headline: Burnham wants a better deal with the EU, with a summit set for 20 November
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham says the way the UK works with the European Union now is not good enough. He told Parliament, where MPs debate and decide things, that it would be wrong not to even look at closer ties. The two sides will meet in Brussels on 20 November.
They may talk about selling food and drink more easily, a scheme that puts a price on pollution, sharing electricity and gas links, a youth experience scheme and working together on immigration. Mr Burnham says he wants the summit to go well first. Bigger questions can wait until later.
He says another vote on the EU is not right at the moment, but he has not said never. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch says he is 'unpicking' the deal that took Britain out of the EU. An EU politician, Bernd Lange, has suggested a 'Switzerland plus' deal. Switzerland is not in the EU, but it has many agreements with it.
Britain left the EU in 2020, so this is a touchy subject.
levels.why: Better ties with Europe could mean easier trade and travel.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister wants closer links with the EU and a meeting is planned for November
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham says Britain's current deal with the European Union is not good enough. He said this to MPs, who are the people elected to make decisions in Parliament. He thinks it would be wrong not to look at getting closer. A big meeting with the EU will be held in Brussels on 20 November.
They could talk about selling food and drink more easily, putting a price on pollution, joining up energy supplies, a youth experience scheme and working together on immigration. Mr Burnham says he wants the meeting to go well first. Bigger choices come later.

levels.why: Closer links could change what we buy, how we travel and who can work where.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister says Britain should work more closely with Europe
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham says the way Britain works with the European Union is not good enough. He told MPs, the people we elect to make decisions, that it would be wrong not to think about getting closer. The EU is a group of European countries that trade and work together. A big meeting will be held in Brussels on 20 November.
They might talk about selling food and drink more easily. They might also talk about sharing energy and a scheme for young people to travel and work abroad. Mr Burnham wants this meeting to go well first. Bigger ideas can come later.
He does not think there should be another vote on the EU right now. He has not said there will never be one. Some people disagree with him. Kemi Badenoch, who leads the Conservatives, says he is undoing the deal that took Britain out of the EU.
Britain left the EU in 2020. People still argue about it.
levels.why: It could make buying and selling goods with Europe simpler.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister wants Britain to be closer friends with Europe
levels.body:
Andy Burnham is the Prime Minister. He is the person in charge of the government. He says the way Britain works with Europe is not good enough. Europe has a group of countries called the European Union, or EU. They share rules and trade with each other. Britain left the EU in 2020.
Mr Burnham wants to talk to the EU again. A big meeting will be held in a city called Brussels on 20 November. They might talk about selling food and drink more easily. They might also talk about sharing energy and helping young people to work and travel abroad.
Some people think this is a good idea. Others do not. Kemi Badenoch leads the Conservatives, a political party. She says he is undoing the choice Britain made when it left.
Mr Burnham says there will not be a new vote about the EU just now. He has not said there never will be.
levels.why: It could change how Britain shares and trades with its neighbours.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister wants to be better friends with our neighbours in Europe
levels.body:
There is a group of countries in Europe called the EU. They trade with each other, which means they buy and sell things. Britain used to be in the group, but it left in 2020. Many people voted for that, and many did not.
Now the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, says things are not good enough. The Prime Minister is the leader of the government. He wants Britain and the EU to work together a bit more. They will have a big meeting in a city called Brussels on 20 November.
They might talk about selling food and drink more easily. They might talk about sharing energy too. They might talk about letting young people work and travel in other countries.
Some people agree with him. Others do not. They say he is undoing what Britain chose. He says he is not planning another vote just yet.
levels.why: It might make it easier to sell and buy things from our neighbours.

levels.headline: Britain wants to be better friends with its neighbours
levels.body:
Imagine your school and the school next door used to share a playground. Then your school decided to stop sharing. Some children thought that was a good idea. Others were sad. Now it has been a few years, and the headteacher thinks the rules for sharing could be better.
This is a bit like what is happening with Britain and the European Union. The EU is a group of countries in Europe. Britain left it in 2020. The person in charge of Britain's government is called the Prime Minister. His name is Andy Burnham.
He says things are not working well enough. So he wants to talk to the EU again. They will meet on 20 November. They might talk about selling food and drink more easily, and about letting young people visit and work in other countries.
Some grown-ups think this is a good idea. Some do not. They are still talking about it.
levels.why: It is about whether neighbours can share more easily.

headline: S&P 500 closes up 0.41% at 7,690.73 as tech stocks rebound from last week's sell-off

terms.meaning: An index tracking the share prices of 500 large US companies, widely used as a gauge of the US stock market.
A stock index dominated by technology companies.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average, an index of 30 large US companies.

levels.headline: S&P 500 closes up 0.41% at 7,690.73 as tech stocks rebound from last week's sell-off
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed up on Monday 19 October, the last completed session, rising 0.41% to 7,690.73. The Nasdaq Composite gained 1.11% to 26,430.89, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.07%, or 36.38 points, to 51,966.03.
The rebound was led by artificial intelligence and chip stocks, with chipmakers recovering after a multi-day slump. It followed a rough week in which the S&P 500 fell nearly 2%, its worst weekly decline since late June, and the Nasdaq dropped about 4.5%.
CNBC reports that analysts remain cautious. Katie Stockton of Fairlead Strategies said this week would be crucial for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq to hold support. About 70 S&P 500 companies are due to report earnings this week, which will help show whether the bounce in technology shares is sustainable.
The Dow's small fall alongside a stronger Nasdaq shows that the gains were concentrated in the technology sector rather than spread across the whole market.
levels.why: Moves in US shares affect pensions, savings and the mood of markets around the world.

levels.headline: US shares rise on Monday as technology stocks bounce back; S&P 500 up 0.41%
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed higher on Monday 19 October, the most recent full trading session, gaining 0.41% to finish at 7,690.73. The Nasdaq Composite rose 1.11% to 26,430.89, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average edged down 0.07%, or 36.38 points, to 51,966.03.
Chip makers and other companies linked to artificial intelligence led the recovery after several days of falls. Last week the S&P 500 lost nearly 2%, its worst week since late June, and the Nasdaq slid about 4.5%.
Analysts are being careful. Katie Stockton of Fairlead Strategies said this week is important if the S&P 500 and Nasdaq are to hold their support levels. Around 70 S&P 500 companies report earnings this week, and these results should show whether the rebound can last.
Because the Dow fell slightly while the Nasdaq jumped, the gains came mostly from technology rather than across the market.
levels.why: Share prices can change the value of savings and pensions for ordinary people.

levels.headline: US stocks rebound on Monday after a tough week for tech

The S&P 500, a measure of 500 big US companies, closed up on Monday 19 October, the last full day of trading. It rose 0.41% to 7,690.73. The Nasdaq, which is full of technology firms, gained 1.11% to 26,430.89. The Dow, which tracks 30 large companies, dipped 0.07% to 51,966.03.

Analysts are cautious. Katie Stockton of Fairlead Strategies said this week matters for whether the market holds its recent support levels. About 70 companies in the S&P 500 will publish their profit figures this week, which should show whether the recovery is real.
The Dow slipped while the Nasdaq rose, so the gains were mainly in technology.
levels.why: Share prices affect pensions and savings, and they show how confident investors feel.

levels.headline: US shares rise on Monday after a rough week, led by technology firms

levels.headline: US shares go up on Monday after a bad week for technology firms
levels.body:
On Monday 19 October, the S&P 500 closed higher. This index follows 500 large US companies. It rose 0.41% to 7,690.73. The Nasdaq, which has many technology companies, rose 1.11% to 26,430.89. The Dow, an index of 30 big firms, fell a little, by 0.07%, to 51,966.03.

levels.headline: US share prices bounced back on Monday, led by tech companies

levels.headline: US share prices went up on Monday after falling last week
levels.body:
A share is a tiny piece of a company. People buy and sell shares, and the prices go up and down. On Monday 19 October, share prices in the United States mostly went up. The S&P 500, which follows 500 big companies, rose by 0.41%. It ended the day at 7,690.73. The Nasdaq, which has lots of technology companies, rose by 1.11%. levels.why: It shows how people feel about money and companies, which can affect pensions.

levels.headline: Share prices in America went up on Monday, but they fell last week
levels.body:
A share is a very small piece of a company. If you own a share, you own a tiny bit of that company. People buy and sell shares all the time, so the prices change. The United States has some of the biggest companies in the world.
On Monday 19 October, many share prices in America went up. A list of 500 big companies, called the S&P 500, went up by a small amount. A list full of technology companies, called the Nasdaq, went up by a bit more. A third list, called the Dow, went down by a tiny amount.
The companies that make computer chips and AI did best. AI means computers that can do clever jobs. Last week their shares had fallen a lot.

levels.why: Share prices show how people feel about companies and money.

levels.headline: Share prices are like prices in a swap shop, and they bounced back on Monday
levels.body:
Imagine a swap shop at school where children trade pieces of famous companies. Each piece is called a share. When lots of children want a piece, its price goes up. When lots want to get rid of it, the price goes down.
On Monday in America, share prices mostly went up. Last week lots of children wanted to get rid of shares in computer and AI companies. AI means computers that can do clever jobs. This week some children came back and bought them again. So the prices went up a little.
The list that follows 500 big companies went up by a little less than half of one in a hundred. The list full of computer companies went up by a bit more than one in a hundred.
This week, about 70 of the big companies will say how much money they made. Grown-ups will watch closely.
levels.why: It shows when people feel happy or worried about money.

headline: Brent crude holds near $110 a barrel as Middle East attacks and Ukrainian strikes on Russian facilities keep supply fears high

terms.meaning: The main international benchmark price for oil, named after a North Sea oilfield.
The main US benchmark price for oil, often shortened to WTI.
A narrow sea passage near Iran through which a large share of the world's oil is shipped.

levels.headline: Brent crude holds near $110 a barrel as Middle East attacks and Ukrainian strikes on Russian facilities keep supply fears high
levels.body:
Brent crude futures closed at $109.55 a barrel on Monday 19 October, down 31 cents, after touching $110.70 earlier in the session. West Texas Intermediate, the US benchmark, rose $2.25 to $103.66.
CNBC reports that prices are being supported by several supply risks. Iran-backed Houthi militants claimed attacks on Saudi airports and Aramco facilities, Ukraine has struck oil facilities in Russia, and Iran has stepped up attacks on tankers in the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman.
Trading Economics data show crude has risen about 11.9% over the past month and about 81% over the past year. Its own forecast, which is a model projection and not a market price, puts Brent near $114 by the end of the quarter.
High oil prices feed through to petrol, diesel, transport and heating costs, and are a key reason inflation has been rising in many countries this year.
levels.why: Oil prices influence petrol, heating and food costs, and can push up inflation and interest rates.

levels.headline: Oil stays close to $110 a barrel as conflict in the Middle East and strikes in Russia threaten supply
levels.body:
Brent crude futures ended Monday 19 October at $109.55 a barrel, 31 cents lower, after reaching $110.70 earlier in the day. The US benchmark, West Texas Intermediate, climbed $2.25 to close at $103.66.
Markets are reacting to several risks to supply. Iran-backed Houthi militants have claimed attacks on Saudi airports and Aramco facilities. Ukraine has hit oil facilities in Russia. Iran has also increased attacks on tankers in the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman.
According to Trading Economics, crude is up about 11.9% in a month and about 81% in a year. It forecasts Brent near $114 by the end of the quarter, although that is a projection rather than an actual price.
Expensive oil raises the cost of fuel, transport and heating, which is one reason inflation has been climbing in many countries.
levels.why: High oil prices can raise bills and prices in the shops, and keep interest rates up.

levels.headline: Oil prices stay near $110 a barrel as supply worries continue
levels.body:
Brent crude, the main global oil price, ended Monday 19 October at $109.55 a barrel, down 31 cents, after briefly reaching $110.70. The main US price, West Texas Intermediate, rose $2.25 to $103.66.

Iran has also attacked more tankers in the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman. The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow sea route that much of the world's oil passes through.

When oil costs more, so does petrol, transport and heating. That is one reason prices in shops have been rising in many countries.

levels.headline: Oil costs about $110 a barrel as attacks in the Middle East and Ukraine worry buyers

Brent crude, the main world oil price, closed on Monday 19 October at $109.55 a barrel, down 31 cents. It had touched $110.70 earlier. The main US price, called West Texas Intermediate, rose $2.25 to $103.66.

levels.headline: Oil is close to $110 a barrel, and fighting in several places is worrying buyers
levels.body:
Oil costs a lot at the moment. On Monday 19 October, a barrel of Brent, the main world oil price, closed at $109.55. A barrel is a large container of oil. The main US price, called West Texas Intermediate, closed at $103.66.

Petrol, diesel and heating cost more when oil does, and shops pass on higher delivery costs.

levels.headline: Oil costs a lot right now, and attacks in different places are the reason
levels.body:
Oil is a thick black liquid dug from the ground. It is used to make petrol and diesel for cars and lorries. On Monday 19 October, one barrel of Brent oil, the main world price, cost $109.55. A barrel is a big container. Last year oil cost much less.
Oil sellers are worried about supplies. Fighters in Yemen called the Houthis, who are backed by Iran, say they attacked airports and oil sites in Saudi Arabia. Ukraine has hit oil sites in Russia. When oil costs more, petrol, delivery and heating cost more too. Shops pass this on.
levels.why: It means petrol, heating and shopping can cost more.

levels.headline: Oil is very expensive now, and fighting in several places is the reason
levels.body:
Oil is a thick liquid from under the ground. It is made into petrol and diesel for cars and lorries. On Monday 19 October, a barrel of the main kind of oil, called Brent, cost about $109. A barrel is a big container. A year ago it cost much less.
People who buy oil are worried because there is fighting in some places that make or move oil. Fighters in Yemen called the Houthis say they attacked airports and oil sites in Saudi Arabia. Ukraine has hit oil sites in Russia. Iran has attacked ships that carry oil.
When less oil can reach buyers, the price goes up. Oil is up by about 12% in one month.
That matters because lorries bring food to shops and homes need heating. So when oil costs more, many other things cost more as well.
levels.why: Dearer oil can make fuel, food and heating cost more.

levels.headline: Oil costs a lot because of fighting in places that make or ship it
levels.body:
Oil is a thick liquid that comes from under the ground. We use it to make petrol and diesel for cars and lorries. A barrel of oil is a big container of it. This week one barrel of the main kind, called Brent, cost about $109. That is a lot more than a year ago.
There is fighting in some of the places that make oil or send it around the world. Fighters in Yemen say they attacked airports and oil sites in Saudi Arabia. Ukraine has hit oil sites in Russia. Iran has attacked ships that carry oil.
When oil gets harder to find, the price goes up. It is like when a toy is hard to find and the shop asks for more money.
Lorries bring food to shops, so higher oil prices can make many things cost more.
levels.why: It can make petrol, food and heating dearer.

levels.headline: Oil is very expensive because there is trouble where it comes from
levels.body:
Oil is a thick black liquid from under the ground. It is made into petrol and diesel for cars and lorries. People pay money for it by the barrel, which is a big container. This week, one barrel cost about $109. That is a lot.
There is fighting in some places that make oil or send it around the world. Some fighters have attacked airports and oil sites in Saudi Arabia. Ukraine has hit oil sites in Russia. Iran has attacked ships that carry oil.
Think about a sweet shop with only a few sweets left. Everyone wants one, so the shopkeeper asks for more money. Oil works like that. When there is less of it, the price goes up.
Lorries use oil to bring food to shops. So when oil costs a lot, shopping and heating can cost more as well.
levels.why: It can make things we buy cost more.

levels.headline: When oil is hard to find, it costs more, like sweets in a sweet shop
levels.body:
Imagine a sweet shop. Normally it has lots of sweets, and they cost a little. Now imagine a storm stops the lorry that brings the sweets. The shop only has a few left. Everyone wants one, so the shopkeeper asks for more money.
Oil works a bit like that. Oil is a thick black liquid from under the ground. It makes petrol for cars and lorries. This week there is fighting in some places that make or carry oil. Some fighters have attacked airports and oil sites in Saudi Arabia. Ukraine has hit oil sites in Russia. Iran has attacked ships that carry oil.
Because oil is harder to get, one barrel now costs about $109. A barrel is a big container.
Lorries carry food to shops. So when oil costs more, lots of things can cost a bit more, and grown-ups worry about it.
levels.why: It shows why fights far away can change prices near us.

headline: Home Secretary says RAF Fairford incident was highly likely co-ordinated from Iran as two Iranian nationals are charged

terms.meaning: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, a powerful branch of Iran's armed forces.
Specialist officers who investigate terrorism offences.
Release of a suspect while an investigation continues, usually with conditions.

levels.headline: Home Secretary says RAF Fairford incident was highly likely co-ordinated from Iran as two Iranian nationals are charged
levels.body:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood told MPs on 12 October that the government's assessment is that the incident near RAF Fairford was highly likely to have been co-ordinated by a known individual based in Iran, and almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Two men, both Iranian nationals, have been charged with terrorism offences.
Five men were arrested on 27 September near the Gloucestershire base. Police said no explosives were found in vehicles seized nearby, although a quantity of petrol was recovered. Further arrests followed, and several men remain on police bail while specialist teams pursue all lines of enquiry.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham had already said there were strong indications that Iran played a part. The Foreign Secretary summoned the Iranian Ambassador. Iran's embassy in London has rejected any involvement and said it strongly condemned speculation linking the country to the alleged plot.
The government has pledged to use its full range of powers against Iran's use of criminal networks and their funding.
levels.why: It raises tensions between the UK and Iran and touches on national security and the safety of military sites.

levels.headline: Government blames Iran-based co-ordination for RAF Fairford incident; two charged with terror offences

levels.headline: Bank of England holds Bank Rate at 3.75% in 6-3 vote as inflation climbs and a November rise looms
levels.body:
The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee voted 6-3 on 17 September to hold Bank Rate at 3.75%. The three members in the minority wanted a 0.25 percentage point rise to 4%.
Governor Andrew Bailey warned that 'the longer this volatility persists, the bigger the impact it will have on inflation, and the more likely it is we will need to raise Bank Rate'. CNBC reported that a rise of at least 0.25 points is widely expected at the next meeting in November.
The Bank is under pressure because inflation has been climbing. The Office for National Statistics said consumer price inflation rose to 3.1% in August, its first move above 3% since March, driven mainly by motor fuel prices, which were up 23% on the year. Core inflation, which strips out volatile items, held at 2.6%.
The next ONS inflation figures, for September, are due on 21 October. The Bank's target is 2%.
levels.why: Interest rates decide how much people pay on mortgages and loans and earn on savings.

headline: Chancellor John Healey to deliver first Budget on 28 October with borrowing running above forecast

levels.headline: Chancellor John Healey to deliver first Budget on 28 October with borrowing running above forecast
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey will deliver his first Budget on Wednesday 28 October. He took over from Rachel Reeves after Andy Burnham became Prime Minister.
The Office for National Statistics reported that public sector borrowing in the financial year to July 2026 was £56.7 billion. That was £6.0 billion, or 9.6%, less than in the same period last year, but £2.3 billion above the forecast of the Office for Budget Responsibility. Borrowing in July alone was £1.8 billion, also above the OBR's forecast.
The Budget will be accompanied by updated OBR fiscal forecasts. Mr Healey and Mr Burnham must balance spending and borrowing against persistent inflation, high government borrowing costs and weak growth. They have not yet set out the full mix of savings or tax measures needed to fund higher defence spending within the government's fiscal rules.
The Budget will therefore be closely watched by markets and households alike.

levels.headline: UK unemployment stood at 4.9% in latest published figures as new ONS labour market data are due
levels.body:
The latest published official figures put UK unemployment at 4.9% for May to July 2026. The Office for National Statistics said that was up 0.2 percentage points on the year but largely unchanged on the latest quarter.
The economic inactivity rate for people aged 16 to 64 was estimated at 20.9%. Regular pay, which excludes bonuses, grew 3.5% and total pay grew 3.9% in the same period. Total pay growth was down from 4.2% in the previous three-month period. After allowing for inflation, regular pay grew 0.8% and total pay 1.1%.
The ONS was due to publish its next labour market update at 7am on 20 October, covering the period to August. We could not confirm those figures at the time of writing. Trading Economics lists forecasts of 4.9% for unemployment and 3.8% for total pay growth.
These numbers matter to the Bank of England as it decides whether to raise interest rates.

levels.headline: France orders partial curfews after weekend of violent cost-of-living protests, with about 2,400 arrests
levels.body:
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has ordered localised, partial curfews after protests over living costs turned violent across France between 17 and 19 October. Reported examples include an 8pm to 6am curfew in four northern cities, including Lille, and a partial curfew with a demonstration ban in parts of Paris. Mr Lecornu has said a state of emergency has not been ruled out.
Around 550,000 people took part in protests, shops were looted and authorities say about 2,400 people were arrested over the weekend. The unrest began with high school protests in poor northern suburbs of Paris over teacher shortages and school conditions, then widened into anger about living costs. Diesel prices have risen nearly 40% and petrol 25% since March.
President Emmanuel Macron condemned the violence but did not declare a state of emergency. He refused the resignation of Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez and ordered a review of planning and intelligence failures. The unrest adds pressure on the minority government ahead of a budget vote on Tuesday.
levels.why: It shows how rising fuel and food prices can spill into unrest and political instability in a major European economy.

levels.headline: US issues rare security alert for citizens in 12 Middle East countries as Houthi attacks on Saudi airports escalate
levels.body:
US embassies across the Middle East issued identical security alerts on Monday 19 October covering 12 countries, including Saudi Arabia. They warn of possible flight cancellations and airspace closures linked to risks from the Houthis and Iran, and say hostilities could escalate rapidly beyond the immediate area.
The alerts follow attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis on Saudi civilian airports and infrastructure. The Houthis claimed strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Abha International Airport on Monday. Officials earlier said a strike on the terminal at Riyadh's airport had killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300. Saudi authorities said airports in Jazan and Najran were targeted on Tuesday.
Separately, the US Federal Aviation Administration has told American airlines to take care around Saudi Arabia, with its warning in effect until 10 December. The attacks come amid the continuing conflict between the United States and Iran, and have helped push oil above $109 a barrel.

levels.headline: China's economy grows 4.5% in third quarter as record exports offset weak property and domestic demand
levels.body:
China's economy grew 4.5% in the third quarter from a year earlier, faster than the 4.3% recorded in the second quarter and ahead of the 4.4% forecast by economists polled by Reuters.
Exports were the main driver. Exports jumped 36.3% year on year to $447.18 billion in September, above the 25.5% expected and the strongest growth in seven months. China recorded a trade surplus of $133.53 billion in the month, with shipments to the United States up sharply. Strong foreign demand for its technology goods more than offset drags from a deepening property slump and sluggish consumer demand.
Fixed asset investment in urban areas fell 7.2% in the first nine months of the year, while retail sales grew 1.1% in September, faster than expected.
Beijing has leaned heavily on exports for growth this year, but that engine faces growing pressure as energy costs surge and its export surge provokes anxiety among trading partners.

levels.headline: Eurozone inflation rises to 3.8% in September, its highest in three years, as energy costs soar
levels.body:
Eurozone annual inflation rose to 3.8% in September from 3.2% in August, above the 3.6% markets expected. It was the highest rate since September 2023, according to CNBC.
Energy was the main driver, with energy inflation reaching 18.8%, its highest since January 2023, as the conflict in the Middle East kept pushing prices up. Core inflation, which strips out volatile items such as energy and food, came in at 2.5%, in line with forecasts.
The European Central Bank raised rates by 0.25 percentage points on 10 September, its second increase this year. Its next decision is on 29 October, and further rises are priced in over the coming year, with the next possibly as early as December. The bank kept its 2026 inflation forecast at 3.0% but raised its projections for 2027 and 2028 to 2.5% and 2.1%.
The euro has also weakened, falling to its lowest level against the US dollar since mid-May 2025, as energy costs and French fiscal worries weigh on it.

levels.headline: US inflation hits 3.7% as Treasury yields stay above 5%; markets expect Fed to hold rates on 28 October
levels.body:
US annual inflation accelerated to 3.7% in September, above forecasts of 3.6%, while core inflation edged up to 2.6%. US producer prices also jumped 1.3% in the month.
The Federal Reserve raised its target range by 0.25 percentage points to 3.75%-4% in September, its first increase since 2023. Sixteen of 18 officials expected another rise this year. Ahead of its next decision on 28 October, traders put the chance of no change above 80%, according to CME FedWatch, while the chance of a December rise has climbed to 92%.
The 10-year Treasury yield rose more than 4 basis points on Monday to about 5.1%, with reports varying slightly by data provider. The 30-year yield was around 5.4% to 5.5%. Yields remain below the highs reached earlier this month, which were the highest since 2002.
Oil is a key factor, as prices have soared this year during the US-Iran conflict, raising fears of persistent inflation.
